    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A latest deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.
    • The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations.
    • According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A latest deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

    Industry observers note that the airline looks to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    According to recent reports, “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano mentioned in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Industry observers note that colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

    Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

    In a recent development, the red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

    Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

    Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

    Recent findings suggest that A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

    It has been revealed that in 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

    Industry observers note that running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch declared he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

    This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

    Center for Security Policy President Tommy Waller warns that a string of outages affecting the NSA, banks and major technology systems raises national security concerns, even as officials rule out a coordinated cyberattack.

    It has been revealed that U.S. adversaries have spent years developing ways to disrupt the country's critical infrastructure in a conflict, and the wave of technology disruptions affecting everything from banks to the National Security Agency has offered a reminder of how detrimental those failures could be even without a cyberattack.

    The string of outages has fueled speculation about whether the incidents are connected, though Trump administration officials have ruled out a coordinated cyberattack.

    National security experts caution that while the outages do not establish malicious activity, they underscore the stakes of protecting systems that underpin everything from financial transactions to military operations.

    TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS.

    "We know that our adversaries use that domain to attack our critical infrastructure," Tommy Waller, a national security expert with the Center for Security Policy, told Fox News Digital.

    "Modern warfare, our people and our critical infrastructures are a prime target for all of our adversaries.".

    Recent findings suggest that china accused the NSA of launching a cyberattack against its national time service. (Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images).

    In a span of six days, technical disruptions affected Microsoft 365, commercial air travel, payroll and human resources software, banking transactions and the National Security Administration's highly classified internal communications network.

    Some led to massive impacts on everyday life, including only the second-ever nationwide ground stop on all commercial flights since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

    "This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation-state," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Tuesday on Fox Business' "The Claman Countdown.".

    Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin similarly insisted the disruptions had "nothing to do with cyberattacks," suggesting that technical failures could become more common as new technology is introduced.

    Industry observers note that "I believe we're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out," Mullin said Tuesday. A day earlier, he sought to reassure Americans during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity," saying, "Well, breathe. The homeland is secure. Our banking system is secure.".

    PRESIDENT TRUMP DOWNPLAYS PANIC OVER TECH OUTAGES: ‘NOBODY’S GOING TO PLAY GAMES WITH US’.

    But the disruption at the NSA, one of the nation's most sophisticated intelligence agencies, has drawn particular scrutiny.

    United Airlines planes parked at Newark Liberty International Airport in Newark, N.J., Nov. 3, 2025. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

    It has been revealed that the agency's highly classified internal communications network, known as NSA Net, went down Tuesday, disrupting employees' ability to communicate classified information internally. Employee attendance at the agency's Fort Meade, Maryland, campus was "staggered" throughout the week to ease systems' use, and the network did not resume operations until Friday.

    "This latest thing at the NSA is more problematic because their systems are generally not tied to anybody else, particularly their classified ones," national security and cybersecurity expert Steve Bucci told Fox News Digital.

    "And, so, that being coincidentally, you know, in this sequence makes it a little harder to just write off.".

    A U.S. official attributed the disruption to routine maintenance, saying the NSA experienced temporary interruptions to some internal systems but that its critical operations and national security capabilities remained fully functional.

    Waller said the NSA outage could have been "self-induced" by efforts to patch vulnerabilities but questioned whether the broader string of disruptions was coincidental.

    "The widespread and persistent nature of it and the types of infrastructures that are being targeted — appear to be targeted — that, to me, claims that it's more than just a coincidence," he mentioned.

    Daniel Hoffman, a former CIA station chief and Fox News contributor, warned the institutions experiencing outages are already prime targets for foreign adversaries and cybercriminals.

    "Every single one of these entities is a target, and so are you and I," Hoffman told Fox News Digital. "Every single day, 24 hours a day, China, Russia, North Korea, Iran, criminals, hackers are trying to target the banks. They're trying to target Microsoft, obviously.".

    Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment.

    It has been revealed that the threat has already reached American infrastructure. In July, hackers targeted more than 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, part of a broader wave of cyber intrusions across multiple states that forced some utilities to switch to manual operations and disrupted water service. Federal investigators examined possible Iranian involvement, though the attacks were not definitively attributed.

    It has been revealed that the Pentagon is also preparing for the possibility of widespread infrastructure failures during a major conflict. Under its FORTRESS initiative, military bases across the continental United States are being directed to prepare to sustain essential operations for at least 90 days without outside support, according to documents previously reviewed by Fox News Digital.

    "We don't want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can't. It's an intolerable risk," Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell previously told Fox News Digital.

    Waller pointed to longstanding Chinese military writings that contemplate attacks on civilian communications and infrastructure during a conflict, arguing that the United States must consider the broader threat even when individual outages appear unrelated.

    It has been revealed that "Again, I am not saying that China did this. But if China wanted to, this is in their doctrine, right?" Waller noted.

    GROCERY STORE CYBERATTACKS ARE ‘PSYCHOLOGICAL WARFARE’ THAT COULD STRIKE US, FORMER FBI AGENT WARNS.

    Industry observers note that in 2024, U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies warned that Chinese state-sponsored hackers known as Volt Typhoon had infiltrated American communications, energy, transportation and water systems, positioning themselves to potentially disrupt critical services during a conflict with the United States.

    Upcoming research published last month found that the group had continued targeting government, defense and critical infrastructure networks through a separate hacking operation, even after U.S. authorities moved to dismantle parts of its infrastructure.

    Bucci, however, noted that an adversary seeking to compromise American infrastructure might have little incentive to cause widespread, visible failures that could expose its activities.

    In a recent development, banking problems and widespread flight disruptions marked a stretch of technology troubles that also hit Microsoft and Workday. (Reuters).

    According to recent reports, "They might want to go in and do things to implant stuff for later use," Bucci noted when asked whether foreign adversaries could be testing vulnerabilities in critical U.S. infrastructure.

    "But you usually don't do a weight test where you make stuff fail or get glitchy because that can then warn the target," he added.

    The disruptions have also prompted calls for greater transparency from federal officials and private companies responsible for critical systems.

    "For our economy to function, people need to have some confidence in banks, among other things," Hoffman mentioned. "So, kind of need to tell us what's going on.".

    Waller also urged greater transparency about infrastructure vulnerabilities and the steps being taken to address them.

    Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

    Recent findings suggest that while I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

    Well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has unveiled prepares to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai.     In a recent development, as is the case for any airline, rolling out a new lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:.

    According to recent reports, emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”.

As you can see, Clark references how the temporary new first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours.
    • The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. We swiftly learned that this happened because L3Harris, a government contractor, was doing maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from copper to fiber.

    The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:.

    Recent findings suggest that so, what’s actually going on here? A latest report sheds some more light on this….

    According to recent reports, CNN has some insights into how little oversight there was of the work being performed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which led to the ground stop disaster that we saw. When was oversight reduced? Well, in early 2025, coinciding with the FAA laying off a large number of employees, as part of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) stunt.

    It has been revealed that according to this report, last Friday morning, an FAA technician escorted a contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control in southern Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician’s belief was that his role was done once the contractor entered the facility, according to people familiar with what happened, plus the union representing FAA employees.

    That router replacement ended up being what triggered the communications complications across the country, ultimately leading to the nationwide ground stop.

    FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford insists that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was performed, but sources dispute that characterization, pointing out that the technician “was only there to unlock the door,” and that “there was no monitoring.”.

    Funny enough, an FAA spokesperson later contradicted Bedford, saying “the FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building,” and “because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work.” It’s amazing how they can’t even keep their narrative straight.

    Industry observers note that this type of hands-off arrangement is apparently a recent development that happened under the Trump administration, and a change to how the FAA used to handle things. In March 2025, an FAA memo laid out changes to how FAA maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, in order to speed things up. The memo stated that “it is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”.

    With this policy, the FAA also went from receiving maintenance “requests” from private contractors that needed to be approved, to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” if not processed in time.

    While the memo claimed that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, there are reportedly only a handful of liaisons nationwide, processing thousands of notifications. In this case, L3Harris reportedly submitted its “notification” with just a few days notice, meaning there was no meaningful oversight.

    A spokesperson for the union representing FAA employees explains that “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”.

    It has been revealed that DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl.

    It also has to be pointed out that the March 2025 memo about a reduction in oversight came just weeks after Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.

    It has been revealed that that’s the beauty of slashing government inefficiency, right? If everything is working well, then we must not need all of those employees, eh? So to have a handful of people being “notified” of work and having to do an analysis sounds like it could be a problem.

    Sources indicate that we have to be honest, in general, politicians are really bad at accountability, and being honest when things go wrong. But whether you like Trump’s policies or not, there’s no denying that he takes lack of accountability to newly introduced levels. Everything good that happens is immediately his doing, and everything bad is Biden’s fault.

    It would be nice if one Trump administration official actually had the introspection to say “hey, let’s make sure this doesn’t happen again,” rather than just yelling “give me $50 billion” and “Biden, Buttigieg, Biden, Buttigieg.”.

    Sources indicate that we’re getting a clearer picture of the circumstances that caused the nationwide ground stop last Friday, the biggest disruption to US air travel since 9/11. A contractor with L3Harris was given access to a site to replace wiring, with virtually no oversight from an FAA employee.

    Recent findings suggest that while the FAA claims that there’s supposed to be oversight of contractor work, in this case the FAA employee was reportedly just tasked with unlocking the door. The approach to overseeing contractor work is reportedly a newly introduced system as of March 2025, where contractor work went from being viewed as “requests” to being viewed as “notifications,” with just a handful of people to oversee these requests. This came just weeks after hundreds of employees were laid off from the FAA, thanks to Musk’s DOGE.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that former Rep.
    • Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.
    • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

    Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

    In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

    As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

    Recent findings suggest that “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

    When McDermott declared his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

    Industry observers note that born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

    Sources indicate that he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

    He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

    Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a newly introduced life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

    It has been revealed that “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

    As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

    Recent findings suggest that then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

    “The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he mentioned in a statement at the time.

    McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

    “Jim McDermott was as significant as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

    #77039. Why All 3 Of Boeing's Most Modern Aircraft Have Drastically Different Wingtip Designs

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1705 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why All 3 Of Boeing's Most Modern Aircraft Have Drastically Different Wingtip Designs

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that boeing's three most modern commercial aircraft, the Boeing 737 MAX, Boeing 787 Dreamliner, and Boeing 777X, share a common objective when it comes to their wing designs: reducing aerodynamic drag and improving fuel efficiency.
    • The differences are not simply a matter of appearance or Boeing experimenting with alternative technologies.
    • Recent findings suggest that an aircraft's wingtips play an key role in determining how efficiently it flies, particularly during cruise.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that boeing's three most modern commercial aircraft, the Boeing 737 MAX, Boeing 787 Dreamliner, and Boeing 777X, share a common objective when it comes to their wing designs: reducing aerodynamic drag and improving fuel efficiency. However, despite pursuing the same goal, all three aircraft feature noticeably different wingtip designs, ranging from distinctive split-tip winglets to swept-back extensions and even enormous folding wingtips.

    The differences are not simply a matter of appearance or Boeing experimenting with alternative technologies. Instead, each design reflects a combination of aerodynamic performance, aircraft dimensions, and the practical limitations imposed by airports. Understanding why these aircraft have such different wingtips provides an interesting insight into the compromises involved in modern aircraft engineering.

    Recent findings suggest that an aircraft's wingtips play an key role in determining how efficiently it flies, particularly during cruise. As air moves around a wing, higher-pressure air beneath the wing attempts to move toward the lower-pressure region above it. This movement creates swirling vortices around the wingtips, which contribute to a phenomenon known as induced drag. The resulting resistance makes it harder for an aircraft to maintain speed and requires additional engine thrust.

    Recent findings suggest that reducing induced drag is therefore a major consideration when manufacturers design new commercial aircraft. One of the most straightforward ways to achieve this is by increasing the wingspan, effectively distributing lift across a longer wing and reducing the strength of the vortices produced at its extremities. However, making wings longer introduces another challenge, since airports have strict limits on how much space aircraft can occupy.

    The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) establishes aircraft size categories that help airports determine which aircraft can use particular gates, taxiways, and other infrastructure. These categories are largely determined by wingspan, meaning manufacturers cannot simply make every aircraft's wings as long as they would ideally like. An aircraft that exceeds the relevant dimensions could require different airport facilities, potentially limiting its operational flexibility.

    Industry observers note that boeing's engineers must consequently balance aerodynamic efficiency against the practical requirements of commercial aviation. Different wingtip devices offer different ways to manage this compromise. Some extend the effective wing vertically, while others increase the actual wingspan or combine both approaches. The three aircraft demonstrate how these engineering decisions can produce substantially different solutions to essentially the same aerodynamic problem.

    In a recent development, the Boeing 737 MAX features perhaps the most visually distinctive wingtip arrangement of the three aircraft. Its Advanced Technology winglets have two separate extensions, with one pointing upward and another extending downward. This split-tip configuration gives the aircraft a distinctive appearance while helping reduce induced drag without requiring a substantial increase in its overall wingspan.

    The reason Boeing selected this particular arrangement becomes clearer when considering the aircraft's relationship with the 737 Next Generation family. The Boeing 737 MAX was developed to retain considerable operational commonality with its predecessors, allowing airlines to introduce the newer aircraft without requiring significant changes to their existing airport infrastructure. Keeping its wingspan within the ICAO Code C limit of 118 feet (36 meters) was therefore an important design consideration.

    A conventional raked wingtip, such as the arrangement found on the Boeing 787, would have extended the 737 MAX's wings too far horizontally. This could have pushed the aircraft outside the dimensions associated with its existing airport category, creating complications for airlines operating it alongside older 737 variants. The split-tip design improved aerodynamic performance while keeping the aircraft within its required dimensional limits.

    The winglets also incorporate carefully shaped surfaces designed to manage airflow and reduce aerodynamic losses. Rather than simply adding extensions to the existing wing, Boeing developed a more sophisticated arrangement intended to improve overall efficiency. This was particularly important for an aircraft that needed to deliver better fuel economy while retaining much of the operational flexibility that had made earlier 737 generations attractive to airlines.

    The latest data from ch-aviation highlights that Southwest Airlines is at the moment the world's largest operator of the Boeing 737 MAX, with a total of 300 in its fleet, followed by United Airlines with 243.

    It has been revealed that unlike the 737 MAX, the Boeing 787 was developed as an entirely upcoming aircraft family, giving Boeing considerably more freedom when designing its wings. Rather than adopting conventional vertical winglets, the manufacturer opted for long, swept-back raked wingtips that extend the wing horizontally. The result is a particularly elegant design that contributes to the 787's distinctive appearance.

    The Boeing 787's wing design was developed with aerodynamic efficiency as a central priority, rather than being constrained by the dimensional requirements associated with an existing narrowbody aircraft family. Its larger wingspan allows the aircraft to benefit from the reduced induced drag associated with longer wings. Boeing was therefore able to pursue a solution that offered aerodynamic advantages without introducing conventional upward-pointing winglets.

    Research from Boeing and NASA indicates that raked wingtips can reduce drag by approximately 5.5%, compared with improvements of around 3.5% to 4.5% for conventional winglets. Although the precise benefits depend on the aircraft and operating conditions, these figures help explain why Boeing selected this configuration for its widebody aircraft. The design also avoids some of the additional structural weight associated with separate winglet structures.

    United Airlines is right now the world's largest operator of the Boeing 787, as outlined in the table below:.

    Sources indicate that another key characteristic of the Boeing 787's wings is their composite construction. Built primarily from advanced carbon-fiber-reinforced materials, they are designed to be long, relatively thin, and flexible. This flexibility allows the wings to respond to aerodynamic forces during flight, while their overall shape contributes to improved efficiency. Combined with the raked wingtips, the design helps the 787 achieve the aerodynamic performance required for long-distance commercial operations.

    According to recent reports, the Boeing 777X takes the concept of longer wings considerably further, featuring the largest wingspan of any commercial airliner at the moment designed for airline service. Its wings extend 235 feet (72 meters) when fully deployed. This substantial span helps reduce induced drag and supports the aircraft's objective of delivering improved fuel efficiency on long-haul routes.

    According to recent reports, however, the Boeing 777X faces a practical problem that the 787 does not encounter to the same extent. Its enormous wingspan would exceed the dimensions permitted within the ICAO Code E category used by many large commercial aircraft. This could make it difficult for the aircraft to operate at airports designed around the existing infrastructure used by conventional widebody aircraft, potentially restricting where airlines could deploy it.

    Industry observers note that boeing's solution was to develop folding wingtips that allow the outer sections of the wings to rotate upward while the aircraft is on the ground. Once folded, the 777X's wingspan is reduced to just under 213 feet (65 m), bringing it within the dimensional requirements associated with Code E airport operations. Before take-off, the wingtips extend into their normal flight positions, restoring the aircraft's full aerodynamic configuration.

    Recent findings suggest that this arrangement is particularly interesting because it allows Boeing to avoid choosing between aerodynamic performance and airport compatibility. The aircraft can benefit from an exceptionally long wing during flight without requiring airports to accommodate its entire wingspan while parked or taxiing. The folding mechanism adds engineering complexity, but it provides a practical solution to a problem that would otherwise have required substantial compromises in wing design.

    The Boeing 777X is set to become the latest and largest member of the manufacturer's successful 777 family. Designed to offer improved efficiency, greater range, and increased passenger comfort, the aircraft will be available in three variants: the 777-8 and 777-9 passenger models, along with the 777-8F cargo aircraft. The Boeing 777-9 will be the first variant to enter service, offering airlines a high-capacity long-haul aircraft. The smaller 777-8 will provide greater range, while the freighter version targets the growing cargo market.

    However, the program has experienced considerable delays. Originally expected to enter service in 2020, the Boeing 777X has faced certification challenges, flight-testing setbacks, and issues involving its fresh GE9X engines. As of November 2026, Boeing is targeting the first 777-9 delivery in 2027. The 777-8F is expected around two years later, while the passenger 777-8 is not anticipated before 2030. Despite the setbacks, the 777X remains an vital part of Boeing's future long-haul aircraft prepares.

    Recent findings suggest that emirates is set to be the world's largest operator of the Boeing 777X, with a staggering 270 on order. The carriers with the largest firm orders for the passenger variants of the 777X (777-8 and 777-9) are outlined in the table below:.

    Although the three Boeing aircraft use different solutions, their wingtip designs are based on the same aerodynamic principles. All three aim to reduce induced drag, improve lift distribution, and lower the amount of energy required to maintain efficient flight. The differences emerge because each aircraft operates within a different set of dimensional and engineering constraints, rather than because Boeing has changed its overall approach to aerodynamic efficiency.

    For the Boeing 737 MAX, airport compatibility was particularly crucial because the aircraft needed to retain the operational flexibility of the previous 737 generation. Its split-tip winglets provide aerodynamic improvements without substantially increasing its wingspan, making them a practical solution for a narrowbody aircraft operating across a wide variety of airports.

    Industry observers note that the Boeing 787 had greater design freedom, allowing Boeing to prioritize aerodynamic performance through a longer wing and swept-back raked wingtips. Its composite construction also makes it possible to develop a lightweight, flexible wing structure that works particularly well with this configuration. The absence of conventional winglets is therefore a deliberate engineering decision, not an omission.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, the Boeing 777X represents a different approach altogether, combining the aerodynamic advantages of an exceptionally long wing with a folding mechanism that addresses airport limitations. Its design demonstrates how manufacturers can use mechanical innovation to overcome restrictions that would otherwise prevent them from pursuing more ambitious aerodynamic improvements.

    Together, these three aircraft show that there is no single ideal wingtip design for every commercial aircraft, since the most effective solution ultimately depends on the aircraft's size, intended operations, and the infrastructure it must use.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age.
    • Recent findings suggest that tampa International Airport (TPA) is building a $1.528 billion terminal that will add 16 gates, a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area for international arrivals, and enough capacity to handle 35 million annual passengers by 2037.
    • Delta signed a 20-year anchor lease for at least six of those gates, including a purpose-built Delta Sky Club lounge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore newly introduced airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

    Recent findings suggest that tampa International Airport (TPA) is building a $1.528 billion terminal that will add 16 gates, a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area for international arrivals, and enough capacity to handle 35 million annual passengers by 2037. Structural steel will begin going up this Summer, with completion targeted for late 2028 and a public opening in 2029. It is the airport's first latest airside terminal in nearly 20 years.

    Delta signed a 20-year anchor lease for at least six of those gates, including a purpose-built Delta Sky Club lounge. The commitment is the longest and most substantial terminal agreement Delta has made at any mid-size Florida airport. It positions Tampa as a potential international gateway for the airline once the new Federal Inspection Services facility gives the airport the processing capacity to support widebody international arrivals.

    TPA is building its first new airside terminal in nearly 20 years. The Hillsborough County Aviation Authority Board approved the 100% final design for Airside D on February 5, clearing the project for full construction. The facility will be 600,000 square feet (55,742 sq meters) with 16 gates serving both domestic and international flights.

    Industry observers note that it includes a latest Federal Inspection Services area for processing international arrivals, an 8-lane security checkpoint, and a new checked baggage inspection system in the main terminal. The total project cost is $1.528 billion, including a $902 million supplemental contract approved in late 2025.

    Recent findings suggest that construction is well underway. A 300-ton crane is erecting the structural steel framework, which consists of 6,200 tons of steel comprising over 7,300 individual pieces connected by 96,000 bolts and 212,000 inches of welding. Approximately 200 workers are on site daily, with that number expected to increase significantly as the project moves from structural work into mechanical, electrical, and interior fit-out phases.

    Recent findings suggest that HNTB designed the project, the same firm that designed TPA's existing main terminal and automated people mover system. Completion is targeted for late 2028 with a public opening in 2029. Once operational, Airside D will increase TPA's total gate count and expand the airport's annual passenger capacity from its current 25 million to 35 million by 2037.

    Sources indicate that the airport handled approximately 24 million passengers in 2024, meaning it is approaching the capacity limits of its existing terminal complex. Airside D provides the infrastructure to accommodate the growth TPA has been experiencing without the crowding and gate constraints that would otherwise limit airline expansion at the airport.

    Recent findings suggest that delta was selected as the anchor tenant for Airside D in a decision unveiled by the Hillsborough County Aviation Authority. The lease covers at least six of the 16 gates on a 20-year term, giving Delta a dedicated presence in the new facility through approximately 2049. The agreement includes a mezzanine-level Delta Sky Club, the carrier's first purpose-built lounge at TPA.

    Recent findings suggest that the remaining 10 gates will be available for other carriers, with the airport authority retaining flexibility to assign them based on demand and airline interest. A 20-year anchor lease at a mid-size airport is not a routine commitment. Delta operates from dozens of airports across the United States, but it signs long-term anchor agreements only at facilities where it intends to build or sustain a significant operation over multiple decades.

    Recent findings suggest that the lease term matches the terminal's useful life, meaning Delta is committing to Tampa for as long as Airside D operates. The Sky Club inclusion signals that Delta expects enough premium traffic at TPA to justify the capital investment and ongoing operating cost of a dedicated lounge, which the airline typically reserves for its largest hubs and busiest focus cities.

    Sources indicate that delta right now operates approximately 45 daily departures from Tampa to destinations including Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis-St. Paul, Salt Lake City, Fresh York-JFK, Boston, and Amsterdam. The Amsterdam route, operated on the A330-900, is Delta's first year-round widebody international service from TPA.

    It serves as a proof of concept for the kind of European flying the airline could expand from Airside D once the facility opens. The six-gate commitment in a terminal with a dedicated Federal Inspection Services area positions Delta to add additional international routes from Tampa without competing for gate space or customs processing capacity in the airport's existing international facility.

    Delta operates the largest domestic hub-and-spoke network of any US carrier. It is built around hubs at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta Airport (ATL), Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP), Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC), Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    In a recent development, atlanta is the largest by a wide margin, handling over 1,000 daily Delta departures and serving as the airline's primary connecting hub for domestic and international traffic. Delta's existing Florida footprint is substantial but spread across multiple airports without a dominant hub presence at any single one.

    The airline operates from Orlando International Airport (MCO), Fort Lauderdale–Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Miami International Airport (MIA), Jacksonville International Airport (JAX), and TPA, among others. None of those airports functions as a Delta hub in the way that Atlanta or Detroit do.

    However, Orlando and Fort Lauderdale carry the highest Florida frequencies, driven by leisure demand from Delta's Northeastern and Midwestern hubs. The anchor tenant commitment does not make Tampa a hub. Delta is not building a connecting operation at TPA comparable to what it runs at Atlanta or Detroit.

    According to recent reports, the lease establishes Tampa as a long-term focus city with dedicated infrastructure, a premium lounge, and the physical capacity to grow well beyond the 45 daily departures Delta currently operates. The distinction matters because a focus city with a 20-year lease and a purpose-built Sky Club receives a different level of investment and scheduling priority than a station where the airline operates from shared gates on short-term agreements.

    TPA already handles international flights. Edelweiss serves Zurich, Avianca recently released daily service to Bogota, and Delta added year-round Amsterdam service. Caribbean and Canadian routes to destinations including San Juan, Toronto, Montreal, Cancun, and Santo Domingo operate from the existing terminal.

    It has been revealed that the airport is not starting international service from zero. What it lacks is the capacity to grow it meaningfully beyond what the current Federal Inspection Services facility can process. Airside D's dedicated FIS area changes that constraint. The newly introduced facility will have its own Customs and Border Protection processing area capable of handling widebody international arrivals simultaneously with domestic operations on the same concourse.

    It has been revealed that delta's six gates in a terminal with FIS capability give the airline the infrastructure to operate international flights from Tampa without competing for processing capacity in the airport's existing international arrivals facility. Routes to London, Paris, or additional European destinations that require a full international arrivals hall become operationally feasible in a way they are not today from Delta's current gate positions.

    The most striking figure in the airport authority's route development materials is the leakage rate. Approximately 50% of Tampa's international origin-and-destination traffic currently uses other Florida airports, primarily MIA, MCO, and FLL.

    Industry observers note that tampa Bay area residents flying internationally drive to other airports because nonstop international options from TPA are limited. Airside D's FIS capacity, combined with Delta's anchor presence and the gate infrastructure to support widebody international service, is designed to recapture that leakage by giving Tampa the facilities to offer the international routes its local market already demands.

    The Tampa Bay metropolitan area is one of the fastest-growing regions in the US. The four-county metro area comprising Hillsborough, Pinellas, Pasco, and Hernando counties has added over 400,000 residents since 2010 and now exceeds 3.3 million people. The region's economy has diversified beyond its traditional tourism and military base.

    Recent findings suggest that indeed, the finance, healthcare, technology, and logistics sectors are driving corporate travel demand alongside the leisure traffic that has historically defined Florida aviation. TPA handled 24.5 million passengers in fiscal year 2025, approaching the 25 million capacity ceiling the airport authority identified as the trigger point for Airside D.

    The 2029 opening timing aligns with several fleet developments at Delta. Namely, Delta's Airbus A350-1000 deliveries will begin in late 2026, freeing up A330-900s and A350-900s that could be deployed on international routes from secondary hubs and focus cities, including Tampa.

    In a recent development, delta's year-round Amsterdam service, rolled out on the A330-900, is a proof of concept for European widebody service from TPA. If the route performs well through 2027 and 2028, additional European destinations from Airside D's gates become a natural extension of the strategy once the facility opens.

    #77033. Industry News: Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (778 w)

    Industry News: Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
    • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

    The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

    He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

    During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

    Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from latest software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin remarked “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

    Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

    “This is an emergency,” he stated. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

    The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

    Mullin remarked the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

    “We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin noted. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

    It has been revealed that thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

    Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

    Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

    Recent findings suggest that the 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

    The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a fresh one was built.

    Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

    “Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell remarked.

    Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

    In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and stated their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

    Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

    Recent findings suggest that at concern in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have remarked they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

    #77032. Breaking: Finnair Celebrates International Men’s Day With All-Male Crew On Flight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (976 w)

    Breaking: Finnair Celebrates International Men’s Day With All-Male Crew On Flight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, there’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female.
    • In a recent development, today is (apparently) International Men’s Day.
    • Industry observers note that the crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, there’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female. Airlines will sometimes have special celebrations with all-female crews, so here’s an interesting twist on that.

    In a recent development, today is (apparently) International Men’s Day. We often see airlines commemorate International Women’s Day, but there aren’t many airlines that celebrate the equivalent for men… well, except Finnair! The airline has today operated its annual flight with an all-male crew. This was the case for Finnair flight AY1331, from Helsinki (HEL) to London (LHR), using an Airbus A350-900.

    Industry observers note that the crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also all men. So, why is this crucial? Finnair highlights how only around 10% of cabin crew at the airline are male, but the organization hopes to see that number grow in the future.

    I think this is a fun concept, and it would be nice to see a closer to 50/50 gender ratio in both the cockpit and cabin, as it would show that everyone is given a fair chance at such a career.

    Industry observers note that I think it’s worth acknowledging that at many airlines, hiring of flight attendants is still primarily or exclusively based on gender. Now, the policies do vary significantly by airline, but perhaps an extreme example is India’s largest airline, IndiGo, which only hires female flight attendants. It’s literally written on the application, that it’s a job for “Female Indian nationals.”.

    It’s all so strange, because the airline has this super enthusiastic page about the importance of diversity in the workplace, and claims “all employment decisions are made solely on the basis of merit and qualifications, without regard to a candidate’s gender…” You mean except the single largest portion of your workforce, which is cabin crew?

    What’s interesting is that while those gender restrictions exist in the cabin, roughly 18% of the carrier’s pilots are female, which is way above the global average of 7%. That’s obviously a conscious effort, so I guess the idea is that women can become pilots but men can’t become flight attendants.

    Industry observers note that in fairness, I suspect part of the motivation here is that IndiGo flight attendants share hotel rooms on layovers, and that is a bit more complicated with mixed genders. Then again, it seems easy enough to just try to pair male flight attendants on trips, so it’s hardly a hurdle that can’t be overcome.

    In a recent development, while we’re used to seeing airlines celebrate International Women’s Day, it’s rare to see an airline celebrating International Men’s Day. Finnair has operated an all-male flight today, intended to highlight how only 10% of flight attendants at the airline are male, and the airline wants to change that. While an unconventional initiative nowadays, I think this is still pretty cool.

    What do you make of Finnair’s all-male flight?

    Amex Auto-Enrolling Card Members In Paperless Billing (Sorry, Dad!)

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….
    • It has been revealed that with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail.
    • We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….

    It has been revealed that with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:.

    We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

    In a recent development, after that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

    In a recent development, now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it says this:.

    Sources indicate that not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

    So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

    Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

    It’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

    So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

    Then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary says something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress….

    As of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that in the early jet era, Lockheed had a full docket of pioneering aerospace programs, but even among the iconic airplanes in the Skunk Works portfolio, the CL-1201 stands out for its scale and ambition.
    • Recent findings suggest that it was a nearly 6,000-ton (5,375 metric tons) flying wing that spanned 1,120 feet (341 meters) in an audacious technical leap to rewrite strategic air mobility and power projection over foreign soil.
    • Although the aerodynamics and physics of constructing such a flying colossus sound like the greatest technical hurdle to its success, the failure of its nuclear power source stopped any progress.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that in the early jet era, Lockheed had a full docket of pioneering aerospace programs, but even among the iconic airplanes in the Skunk Works portfolio, the CL-1201 stands out for its scale and ambition. Locked in the endlessly escalating arms race with the Soviet Union, the US Air Force has commissioned an engineering study into a flying, nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. On September 12, 1969, Lockheed engineers G. Daniel Brewer, S. Dalton, and P. J. Sibley filed a company report LR-22802, outlining a machine that seemed to defy physics.

    Recent findings suggest that it was a nearly 6,000-ton (5,375 metric tons) flying wing that spanned 1,120 feet (341 meters) in an audacious technical leap to rewrite strategic air mobility and power projection over foreign soil. The mothership was expected to haul at least 22 McDonnell Douglas fighter jets on massive underwing pylons in the same way that the smaller planes carried missiles. Designated the CL-1201, the behemoth 'lightning' carrier would be capable of reaching any conflict zone in hours and promised to cruise for 41 straight days without resupply.

    Although the aerodynamics and physics of constructing such a flying colossus sound like the greatest technical hurdle to its success, the failure of its nuclear power source stopped any progress. Popular accounts of the program claim that the USAF did in fact commission an active service example. However, no records to date, including the most detailed public file NASA, recorded as Memorandum X-2386, show that any order was officially lodged.

    The CL-1201's propulsion abandoned standard jet fuel logistics in favor of an unproven liquid-metal-cooled reactor delivering 1,830 megawatts of thermal energy. That staggering heat drove four mammoth aft turbofans at Mach 0.8 at 30,000 feet (9,144 meters), offering effectively unlimited global range. The design aimed to bypass the need for any overseas airfields and reliance on allied partners entirely by maintaining an airborne presence for over a month, limited only by crew endurance and engine oil.

    The primary CL-1201-1-1 Attack Aircraft Carrier variant would house a crew of 845 to operate 22 fighters beneath its wings. Meanwhile, the alternative CL-1201-1-3 Logistics Support Aircraft traded strike fighters for a cavernous cargo bay. It was proposed with the capacity to deploy an entire combat brigade of 3,896 soldiers with 6,207 tons (5,631 metric tons) of equipment to any hot spot on the globe.

    Industry observers note that eight years before Lockheed's engineers filed their report, US President John F. Kennedy had already canceled the US aircraft nuclear propulsion program. After 15 years of research, it was finally called off in 1961. The numbers had never successfully solved all the safety issues with installing an active nuclear reactor in an airplane. Two airships, the USS Akron and Macon, preceded the C-1201 as early motherships, and one Convair NB-36H had been equipped with nuclear power plants for test flights.

    Industry observers note that yet, scientists were unable to ever create an atomic engine considered safe enough to not have a devastating environmental impact in the event of a mishap. Furthermore, turning the CL-1201 concept into an airworthy airframe demanded solving the immediate physics problem of how to lift nearly 12 million lb (5.4 million kg) into the sky. No airport on Earth could handle the landing gear footprint, forcing the design team to adopt a complex propulsion compromise.

    Sources indicate that the retrieval system of the CL-1201 lowered a hydraulically stabilized pantograph hook 35 feet (10.7 meters) beneath the airframe into clean, undisturbed air. A docking fighter pilot engaged the hook with a dorsal latch, allowing heavy winches to haul the aircraft up against cradle stops before swinging it into internal maintenance bays. This acrobatic aerial recovery demanded precision flying in high-altitude crosswinds, turning routine combat patrols into dangerous flight-test maneuvers that risked pilot lives.

    According to recent reports, docking a 40,000-lb (18,140 kg) fighter beneath a 125,000-square-foot (11,613 sq m) wing generated lethal aerodynamic turbulence that tested the limits of human piloting. Incoming flight crews had to fly through a violent boundary layer wake and wingtip vortex wash, with velocity spikes exceeding 120 feet (37 meters) per second. The chaotic upwash threatened to smash approaching jets against the lower wing skin, prompting designers to engineer an articulated trapeze boom.

    Beyond the docking challenges, Cold War missile advances made the carrier extraordinarily vulnerable to long-range Soviet surface-to-air missile networks. The tailless 560-foot (171-meter) airframe would look like staring into the sun on an enemy's radar scope. Its gigantic profile would create an immense radar target that air defense systems like the Soviet S-200 Angara could spot hundreds of miles away. A single missile strike could instantly wipe out an entire combat wing and crack open the central atomic reactor.

    At a gross weight of 11.85 million lb (5.4 million kg), roughly fifteen times the mass of a Boeing 747 or Lockheed C-5 Galaxy, the CL-1201 exceeded the limits of every runway in the world. Standard concrete aprons would be crushed under its landing gear, while constructing dedicated five-mile runways around the world negated the strategic autonomy that justified it. To eliminate runway dependence, engineering lead Brewer and his team adopted an extreme vertical takeoff and landing design.

    According to recent reports, rather than routing reactor thermal energy to lift fans, the configuration housed 182 dedicated jet-fuel-powered turbojets in retractable forward fuselage bays and inner wing banks. It would dramatically scale up the multi-engine vertical lift concept of experimental aircraft at the time, like the Dornier Do 31 and Yakovlev Yak 38. Each turbine was rated for 90,000 pounds of thrust for a combined vertical output of 16.38 million pounds.

    In operational practice, this propulsion created severe liabilities at every launch site. Simultaneous ignition of 182 lift jets projected a 1,400°F downward exhaust plume capable of spalling reinforced concrete, liquefying asphalt, and generating severe foreign object damage hazards across massive areas. Furthermore, the lift engines would consume nearly 1.9 million lb (0.8 million kg) of JP-5 fuel during a single five-minute departure sequence, burning the equivalent fuel capacity of six fully loaded C-5 Galaxies before the nuclear engines engaged.

    It has been revealed that additionally, synchronizing 182 independent turbines during the low-speed transition from jet-borne hover to wing-borne aerodynamic flight introduced an alarmingly long list of potential failure points. A compressor stall or flameout within an outboard wing bank would generate violent asymmetric roll moments far exceeding the control authority of aerodynamic flight surfaces at near-zero airspeed. Ultimately, the CL 1201 was simply unviable due to its inability to break away from conventional infrastructure and limitations because of its size and not its power source, relegating the concept to a Cold War 'flight of fancy.'.

    In a recent development, in the 1940s and 1950s, the USAF and Atomic Energy Commission spent roughly $1 billion over 15 years on the Aircraft Nuclear Propulsion (ANP) program, hoping to build bombers that could stay airborne for weeks. The Convair NB-36H Crusader flew 47 test missions over Texas and Fresh Mexico carrying an operational, air-cooled 1-to-3 megawatt reactor in its aft bomb bay. The bomber's entire nose had a 12-ton lead and rubber shield, complete with 12-inch-thick lead-glass windows.

    Adding the 17.5-ton reactor meant the aircraft had to haul nearly 30 tons of nuclear hardware and shielding before carrying any weapons. Every test flight was shadowed by a C-97 transport plane carrying a platoon of US Marines trained to parachute into the crash site and cordon off radioactive debris. Engineers could not solve the dilemma of making a reactor light enough without sacrificing containment. Furthermore, advances in intercontinental ballistic missiles and aerial refueling made nuclear bombers strategically obsolete.

    According to recent reports, lockheed aimed to overcome those limitations with an atomic propulsion plant rated at an astonishing 5,470 megawatts in a dual-circuit closed loop. Liquid lithium circulated through the primary reactor core at temperatures reaching 2,000°F (1,093°C), carrying thermal energy into an intermediate heat exchanger mounted inside a central structural containment cell. The secondary circuit circulated non-radioactive liquid alloy through pipes to four massive trailing-edge turbofans.

    The engines used single-stage titanium fan disks spanning an unprecedented 28 feet (8.5 meters) across. The liquid metal radiators sat directly behind the 14-stage axial compressors, transferring heat into the compressed air stream to produce 300,000 pounds of thrust (1,334 kN) per engine. Containing the energy required a titanium keel and trusses that were eight inches (20 cm) thick, as well as a shield of lead, tungsten, and borated water weighing 1.2 million lb (544,300 kg).

    In a recent development, commissioned in the early 1930s, the USS Akron (ZRS-4) and her sister ship USS Macon (ZRS-5) were 785-foot-long rigid helium airships. Each airship housed an internal hangar bay holding up to five Curtiss F9C-2 Sparrowhawk biplanes. To launch, a mechanical 'trapeze' lowered a fighter beneath the airship's hull into the slipstream, where the pilot released a skyhook and flew away. To recover, the pilot matched the airship's 70-knot speed and snagged the trapeze bar with a hook mounted above the upper wing.

    Industry observers note that on April 4, 1933, the Akron was caught in a violent thunderstorm off the coast of New Jersey. Downdrafts forced the tail into the Atlantic Ocean, breaking the airship apart. Less than two years later, on February 12, 1935, the Macon encountered a storm off Point Sur, California. Wind shear tore away her upper tail fin, puncturing rear gas cells and causing her to lose buoyancy and settle into the Pacific.

    Before the tragic and catastrophic demise of each airship, the trapeze system actually worked well, and the Navy never lost a plane during an in-flight catch. Despite successful fighter operations, the loss of the Macon ended the US Navy's permanent pursuit of flying aircraft carriers, and there's no indication that they ever showed interest in the massive Lockheed concept. Meanwhile, the CL-1201 aimed to take this ill-fated earlier attempt and supersize it.
